blocks.text: A 19-year-old rugby player is carried off with a deformed, swollen shin. His foot is warm and pink on arrival, but four hours after a cast is applied he is begging for more morphine and his toes hurt when you move them. The fracture was the easy part; what comes after is where limbs are lost.

blocks.markdown: **Describing a fracture.** A radiograph is described in a fixed order so that nothing is missed and the surgeon on the phone can picture it. Always obtain **two views at right angles** (anteroposterior and lateral) and include the **joint above and the joint below** a long-bone fracture, because injuries often occur in pairs (for example a forearm fracture with a dislocated elbow or wrist).

blocks.title: A systematic description
blocks.text:
1. **Site**: which bone, and which part (proximal, middle or distal third; diaphysis, metaphysis, epiphysis or growth plate in children).
2. **Pattern**: transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted (more than two fragments), segmental, impacted, avulsion, compression; in children greenstick or buckle (torus).
3. **Displacement** of the distal fragment relative to the proximal: *translation* (shift, in percent of bone width), *angulation* (the direction the apex points or the distal part points, in degrees), *rotation* and *shortening*.
4. **Joint involvement**: intra-articular extension, dislocation or subluxation.
5. **Open or closed**, and associated soft tissue or neurovascular injury.

rows: Fracture line at right angles to the shaft
Direct force; usually stable once reduced
Twisting force; may shorten and be unstable without fixation
Incomplete cortical break in a child's pliable bone
Needs anatomical reduction to limit post-traumatic arthritis
Fracture communicates with the exterior via a wound
blocks.caption: Common descriptive terms

blocks.title: Worked example: describing a distal forearm radiograph
blocks.prompt: A radiograph of a 66-year-old woman who fell on an outstretched hand shows a fracture of the distal radius with the distal fragment displaced dorsally by 6 mm relative to a radial shaft width of 20 mm, tilted dorsally by 20 degrees, with no joint line step. The ulna is intact. Write the description.

steps.text: Site: distal third of the radius; the metaphysis is the usual region in older adults.
Pattern: single transverse or short oblique line without comminution, as described.
Displacement: translation = 6 mm / 20 mm x 100 = 30 percent of the shaft width dorsally; angulation = 20 degrees dorsal tilt (apex volar); no rotation or shortening is described.
Joint: no intra-articular step, so this is extra-articular; the wrist radiocarpal and distal radio-ulnar joints are checked on the lateral and AP views.

Open or closed: closed (no wound described). The ulna is intact; this pattern is commonly called a Colles-type fracture, and a displaced example is usually reduced under local or regional anaesthesia.

blocks.answer: Closed, extra-articular, dorsally displaced and angulated distal radius fracture with 30 percent translation; reduction is considered.

blocks.markdown: **Principles of treatment: reduce, hold, rehabilitate.** *Reduction* restores alignment: closed reduction by traction and manipulation under analgesia or anaesthesia (for example a haematoma block or regional block), or open reduction when closed attempts fail or the fracture is intra-articular, where anatomical reduction is needed. *Immobilisation* maintains reduction: a plaster or synthetic cast (which holds by three-point fixation and should include the joint above and below), a backslab (a half-cast that allows for swelling), traction, or internal or external fixation. *Rehabilitation* restores function: early movement of adjacent joints, weight-bearing as the fixation allows and physiotherapy. Healing goes through haematoma, soft callus, hard callus and remodelling; it is faster with good blood supply, stability and in children.

rows: Stable or reduced fractures, many paediatric fractures
Stiffness, pressure sores, swelling inside a tight cast, compartment syndrome
Intra-articular and forearm fractures needing anatomical reduction
Rod inside the medullary canal shares load
Pins through skin linked by frame
Open fractures with soft tissue damage, damage control in polytrauma

blocks.title: Neurovascular assessment
blocks.text: Document **before and after** any reduction, splint or cast: colour, warmth, capillary refill, distal pulses, sensation in each nerve territory and active movement. A pale, pulseless, cold limb after a fracture or dislocation is limb-threatening: gently realign the limb in the emergency department, reassess the pulses and call the vascular and orthopaedic teams urgently, rather than waiting for repeated radiographs.

blocks.title: Open fractures and grading
blocks.text: Gustilo-Anderson classification: **Type I** wound under about 1 cm and clean; **Type II** about 1 to 10 cm without extensive soft tissue damage; **Type III** extensive soft tissue damage, usually over about 10 cm, or high-energy or contaminated injuries, subdivided into **IIIA** (adequate soft tissue cover), **IIIB** (periosteal stripping and bone exposed, needs flap cover) and **IIIC** (arterial injury needing repair). The wound size cut-offs are a guide; the grade is assigned at debridement. Management follows national standards such as BOAST and NICE: antibiotics as soon as possible and ideally within one hour of injury, tetanus prophylaxis, photograph and saline-soaked dressing of the wound, splint, then early surgical debridement with orthopaedic and plastic surgical cover plan. Check antibiotic choice and doses against current BNF and local guidance.

blocks.title: Worked example: a 4 cm open wound
blocks.prompt: A 31-year-old cyclist has an open tibial shaft fracture with a 4 cm wound, moderate contamination and no flap needed. Foot pulses are present. Outline first-hour management and grade.

steps.text: Grade: the wound is between about 1 and 10 cm, without extensive soft tissue loss or arterial injury, so Gustilo-Anderson type II (the final grade is given at surgery).
Resuscitate with ATLS principles; assess and document neurovascular status; control bleeding with direct pressure.
Antibiotics according to local protocol (check BNF/BOAST) as soon as possible, ideally within the first hour; confirm tetanus cover.
Photograph the wound, apply a saline-soaked dressing, realign and splint, and do not repeatedly probe or take the dressing down.
Arrange urgent theatre for irrigation, debridement and stabilisation (for example intramedullary nail or external fixation), with plastic surgical input if cover is needed.

blocks.answer: Gustilo-Anderson type II open tibial fracture; antibiotics within the first hour, splint, and urgent debridement and stabilisation.

blocks.markdown: **Compartment syndrome.** Muscles lie in closed fascial compartments. Swelling or bleeding raises the pressure inside until capillary perfusion falls, producing muscle and nerve ischaemia. It follows tibial shaft and forearm fractures, supracondylar fractures in children, crush injuries and tight casts or dressings. The earliest and most important sign is **pain out of proportion** to the injury, not relieved by usual analgesia, and **pain on passive stretch** of the muscles in the compartment; the compartment feels tense. Paraesthesia, pallor, pulselessness and paralysis are late signs, and a palpable pulse does not exclude the condition. Children may show increasing analgesia requirement, agitation and anxiety. Management: remove or split every circumferential dressing and cast to skin, keep the limb at heart level, give analgesia and oxygen, avoid hypotension, and arrange **urgent fasciotomy** if symptoms persist. Compartment pressure measurement can help in an unconscious patient or when the diagnosis is uncertain.

blocks.caption: Perfusion pressure (mmHg) across the compartment. Many protocols treat $\Delta P$ of 30 mmHg or less as an indication for fasciotomy; thresholds vary, and the clinical picture decides.

points: Describe a fracture by site, pattern, displacement (translation, angulation, rotation, shortening) and joint involvement, using two views and the joints above and below.

Treatment is reduce, hold and rehabilitate: closed or open reduction, immobilisation by cast, traction or fixation, and early rehabilitation; intra-articular and unstable fractures usually need surgery.
Open fractures need early antibiotics, splintage and surgical debridement, graded by Gustilo-Anderson; document neurovascular status before and after every manoeuvre.
Compartment syndrome is a clinical diagnosis based on pain out of proportion and pain on passive stretch; treatment is releasing constricting casts and urgent fasciotomy.

questions.stem: A junior doctor requests only a single anteroposterior radiograph of a patient's mid-shaft tibial fracture. Which statement about adequate assessment is correct?

options.text: Two views at right angles that include the knee and ankle joints are required
A single AP view is sufficient if the fracture is obvious
Only the joint nearer the fracture needs imaging
Radiographs are unnecessary if the limb is deformed

questions.correctOptionText: Two views at right angles that include the knee and ankle joints are required

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this avoids missing angulation, associated joint injury or a second fracture.
distractorRationale.b: A single view can hide angulation and displacement.
distractorRationale.d: Imaging defines pattern and guides treatment.

questions.explanation: Fractures are three-dimensional, so two orthogonal views are required, and the joints above and below must be seen to exclude associated injury, which is common in the forearm and tibia. Radiographs also let the surgeon plan reduction and fixation.

questions.stem: A radiograph of a displaced humeral shaft fracture shows the distal fragment translated laterally by 9 mm. The width of the humeral shaft at that level is 24 mm. Express the translation as a percentage of the shaft width.
questions.explanation: Translation as a percentage = 9/24 x 100 = 37.5 percent. Expressing displacement relative to bone width, with angulation in degrees, allows consistent description between clinicians.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old falls from a ladder and a radiograph shows a displaced fracture with a step in the articular surface of the distal tibia. What is the best treatment principle?

options.text: Anatomical reduction, usually with open reduction and internal fixation
Accept any position because union will still occur
Immobilise in a cast without reduction
Early unrestricted weight-bearing

questions.correctOptionText: Anatomical reduction, usually with open reduction and internal fixation

distractorRationale.b: Joint incongruity leads to early arthritis.
distractorRationale.c: This leaves the articular surface displaced.

questions.explanation: Intra-articular fractures need restoration of a smooth articular surface to reduce the risk of post-traumatic osteoarthritis, so anatomical reduction and stable fixation (ORIF) are usually required. A cast alone cannot restore a displaced joint surface.

questions.stem: After closed reduction and application of a cast, the limb's neurovascular status should be reassessed and documented, and a check radiograph taken to confirm alignment.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Reduction and immobilisation can stretch or compress vessels and nerves and swelling may subsequently develop, so repeat neurovascular checks and imaging confirm that the reduction has been maintained. These findings should be documented before discharge.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy with a supracondylar humerus fracture treated in a full cast becomes progressively agitated overnight and requires increasing doses of analgesia. His fingers are pale and he cries when they are passively extended. Which is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Split the cast and padding down to skin, elevate to heart level and call for urgent senior review
Give more analgesia and re-check in the morning
Reassure the parents that this is normal cast discomfort
Elevate the arm well above heart level and apply ice

questions.correctOptionText: Split the cast and padding down to skin, elevate to heart level and call for urgent senior review

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is suspected compartment syndrome.
distractorRationale.c: Pain with passive stretch in this setting is not normal.
distractorRationale.d: Elevation above heart level worsens perfusion; cooling is not advised.

questions.explanation: Increasing analgesic requirement, agitation and pain on passive finger stretch inside a tight cast suggest compartment syndrome in a child. Releasing all circumferential dressings immediately and urgent senior assessment for fasciotomy are needed.

questions.stem: A man with a tibial fracture has a diastolic blood pressure of 68 mmHg and an intracompartmental pressure of 41 mmHg. Calculate the compartment perfusion pressure, delta P, in mmHg.
questions.explanation: Delta P = diastolic pressure minus compartment pressure = 68 - 41 = 27 mmHg. Many protocols use a delta P of 30 mmHg or less as supportive of fasciotomy, but the clinical picture is decisive and thresholds vary.

questions.stem: A 40-year-old motorcyclist has an open tibial fracture with a 14 cm wound, exposed bone stripped of periosteum, and gross contamination. Debridement shows that a free flap will be needed for cover. The foot pulses are normal. What is the Gustilo-Anderson grade?

options.text: Type IIIB
Type I
Type II
Type IIIC

distractorRationale.a: Correct: extensive soft tissue loss with periosteal stripping needing flap cover.
distractorRationale.c: Moderate wound without extensive soft tissue damage.
distractorRationale.d: Requires an arterial injury needing repair.

questions.explanation: A large contaminated wound with periosteal stripping and bone exposure that needs flap coverage is type IIIB. Type IIIC needs vascular injury requiring repair, which is absent here as the pulses are normal.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old has a displaced ankle fracture-dislocation after a fall. The foot is cold and pale with no palpable dorsalis pedis or posterior tibial pulse. What is the most appropriate immediate step?

options.text: Gentle realignment of the ankle with prompt reassessment of pulses and call vascular and orthopaedic teams
Wait for CT angiography before touching the limb
Apply a tight circumferential cast and review tomorrow
Give oral analgesia and discharge

questions.correctOptionText: Gentle realignment of the ankle with prompt reassessment of pulses and call vascular and orthopaedic teams

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the limb is threatened and reduction often restores flow.
distractorRationale.c: A cast does not treat vascular compromise.

questions.explanation: A dislocated ankle can kink or compress arteries, and realigning the limb often restores perfusion at once. The limb should be re-examined after reduction and urgent vascular and orthopaedic input arranged if pulses do not return.

questions.stem: Outline the principles of fracture management (reduction, immobilisation and fixation) and give four situations in which surgical fixation is preferred to a cast.
markingGuide: Reduction: closed (manipulation under analgesia/anaesthesia) or open when closed fails or anatomical alignment is needed
Immobilisation: cast, backslab, traction; three-point fixation; include joint above and below
Fixation: plates and screws, intramedullary nail, K-wires, external fixator

Surgical indications (any four): unstable or comminuted, intra-articular displacement, open fracture, failed closed reduction, neurovascular injury, polytrauma, pathological fracture, need for early mobilisation
questions.explanation: Strong answers present the sequence reduce, hold, rehabilitate and then state why internal fixation is chosen when stability or joint congruity cannot be maintained by a cast.

questions.stem: You are shown a radiograph of the right tibia and fibula. Describe the fracture systematically, using the following findings: an oblique fracture line in the middle third of the tibial shaft, the distal fragment shifted medially by half the shaft width, 10 degrees of varus angulation, an intact fibula, and no joint line disruption.
markingGuide: Site: middle third of the right tibial shaft
Pattern: oblique, closed (if no wound), single line (not comminuted as stated)
Displacement: medial translation 50 percent of shaft width; 10 degrees varus angulation; mention rotation and shortening
Fibula intact; no joint involvement, but joints above and below must be seen on two views
Stating that the open or closed status and neurovascular status must be documented
questions.explanation: A systematic approach states the bone and level, the line, the position of the distal fragment relative to the proximal, any joint involvement and whether the injury is open. A good answer notes that two views and the joints above and below are needed to complete assessment.
